children: By Dalvin Brown

When John Bonadeo called Social Security to inquire about collecting his benefits, the representative asked whether he had any children under the age of 18. That question unlocked a gusher of government money that he hadn't known existed.

Bonadeo, a semiretired general contractor who is now 72, and Betty McDonald had six children they had adopted in their 50s. The youngest was 2 years old. Bonadeo's Social Security benefits came with an additional roughly $600-a-month benefit for his children, he said.
"We were really floored," said McDonald, 69, a retired Secret Service agent who lives in Del Mar, Calif. The family needed the money while all the children were still young, she said.

There are more older parents than ever, and they are learning-sometimes by surprise-about Social Security's dependent benefit. Once a parent or grandparent with a dependent files, a child generally can collect up to half of the full retirement-age benefit until they turn 18, or 19 if they are still in high school. The federal agency doesn't market it widely, but it can alter the calculus about when to draw benefits.

The number of households headed by someone 65 or older with a child under 18 has more than tripled between 2000 and 2024, to about 410,000, census data show. Children collecting on retired workers' records grew by about a quarter over roughly the same span, to 323,000 as of December 2024, though it has fallen in the past few years, according to Social Security data.

Americans can begin collecting Social Security between the age of 62 and 70, but their benefits generally go up the longer they wait to start. In recent years, fewer people have been claiming at age 62.

The dependent benefit complicates this calculus. Parents pursuing the benefit generally collect more months of payments for their children the earlier they collect. Waiting means fewer or no payments before a child ages out, but can mean a bigger monthly check for the parent over the rest of their life.

Deciding when to draw the benefit turns on how long a child has left to collect, how long the parent expects to live, whether a second parent can file instead and when the family's biggest expenses arrive.

Elaine Floyd, a certified financial planner at Horsesmouth, gave the example of a husband and wife, both 62, with an 8-year-old. She assumed full-retirement age benefits of $3,800 for the husband and $2,500 for the wife. If both claimed at 62, the child could collect for 10 years, versus two if both parents waited until 70. Both filing immediately would reduce the husband's check to $2,676 and the wife's to $1,760. The child would receive $1,900-half the husband's full retirement age benefit.

If the husband lives to age 88 and the wife to 91, the model still projects more lifetime benefits if both wait because their retirement checks would be larger. They would get about $2.78 million over their lifetimes, versus $2.26 million, a difference of roughly $520,000.

While children can collect as much as 50% of the parent's benefit, there is a family maximum that caps the total payout, regardless of how many qualifying children they have. It generally runs from 150% to 188% of the parent's full benefit, and the parent's own payment counts first.

Phillip Nieburg, a retired pediatrician and epidemiologist, had children at age 44, 49 and 52. Nieburg, now 82, of Charlottesville, Va., filed between 62 and 63, limiting his check for life so his two youngest could collect. His oldest was eligible, too, but a third child wouldn't have increased the family's total.
The two younger children received just under $1,000 a month between them. The money went into their two college accounts and reduced the family's borrowing for three tuition bills.
By his calculation, waiting would have given him more money if he lived past 80 or 81, he said. Nieburg said he would make the same choice again.
"It did provide the money when we needed it," he said.

The longer you live, the more it typically makes sense to wait to collect, said Laurence Kotlikoff, a Boston University economist whose company sells Social Security claiming software. His 2023 study found that, among households headed by workers age 45 to 62, more than 90% would come out ahead if the workers waited until 70 to claim.

Kotlikoff said couples can stagger their claims. The lower earner can file early to start the child's payments while the higher earner waits, preserving the larger future retirement check. When the higher earner files later, the child moves to that record and the check size rises.
Some parents said they value having the additional money more while their children are still at home, when costs of living tend to be higher anyway.

Dawn Lyons, a federal contractor in New Orleans who turns 60 next month, is leaning toward filing early once she is eligible. She plans to claim in October 2028, when she turns 62 and her daughter, now 16, will be a high-school senior. Lyons expects her daughter could collect for less than a year, but the money could help with college.

Lyons mainly wants to claim before Congress makes any changes to the Social Security program if it moves to bolster the solvency of the fund, which is slated to run out of money in 2032. She theorizes that an overhaul would spare people already receiving benefits. Filing at 62 would permanently reduce her benefit, but she is OK with that.
"I want to live my life," she said. "I don't want to work and die."
